fixes.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. The royal servants bowed to Haman, the man King Xerxes had honored, "…because the king had commanded that this be done for him." The order came from King Xerxes himself. Closest I ever got to a bow was a rubber band flopping over in the junk drawer I used to live in.
The verse says the opposite, friend. The royal servants bowed down, "But Mordecai would not bow down or pay homage." Mordecai is the one who refuses. The servants bow, and he doesn't.

Right, he doesn't. The royal servants bowed down to Haman, "But Mordecai would not bow down or pay homage." One man refuses while the royal servants bow. I bet that gate felt awfully quiet in that moment.
Jew is right. The text says Mordecai "…had told them he was a Jew." The servants reported Mordecai to Haman, and Mordecai had said it plainly. That detail ends up mattering a lot.
That's not what the text says, friend. It says Mordecai "…had told them he was a Jew." Persian is a fine word, but it isn't the one in this verse.
Egyptian isn't in this verse at all. The text says Mordecai "…had told them he was a Jew." Nobody in this passage is talking about Egypt.

The text names a different target, friend. It says Haman "…sought to destroy all of Mordecai’s people, the Jews, throughout the kingdom of Xerxes." That's a whole people, not a group at one gate. Haman's plan was far bigger than that.

Yes, the twelfth month. The text says, "…the lot fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar." The lot was cast in the first month, so the month it picked comes much later in the year. Lots of calendar between the casting and that month.

Not the second, friend. The text says the lot "…fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar." The lot was cast in the first month, but it landed on a month much later. Think of it as a calendar page flipped way ahead.
Seventh isn't the one. The lot "…fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar." The twelfth month is the one the text names. The pick lands far from where it was cast.

Haman never names them. He says, "There is a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples of every province of your kingdom." He goes on to talk about their laws, but he never says who they are. I think that's worth noticing.

That's his claim. Haman says, "Their laws are different from everyone else’s, and they do not obey the king’s laws." Notice it's what Haman says about them. He follows it with, "So it is not in the king’s best interest to tolerate them."

Bronze isn't the metal in the text. Haman says, "…I will deposit ten thousand talents of silver into the royal treasury to pay those who carry it out." Silver is the answer, friend. Ten thousand talents of it.

The signet ring! The text says the king "…removed the signet ring from his finger and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews." Verse 12 says the order was "sealed with the royal signet ring." I think handing it over is a big deal.

No crown here, friend. The text says the king "…removed the signet ring from his finger…" A ring off the finger is what changes hands. I think a king handing over that ring is still a very big moment.
Not only Aramaic, friend. The text says the order was written "…in the script of each province and the language of every people." That covers more than one language.

Not just Hebrew, friend. The text says the order was written "…in the script of each province and the language of every people." Hebrew isn't even named in the verse. It goes well beyond one language.

Look at the name on it. The text says, "It was written in the name of King Xerxes and sealed with the royal signet ring." So the king's name and the king's ring were on it. That's the ring Haman had been handed back in verse 10.

That's right. The text says, "It was written in the name of King Xerxes and sealed with the royal signet ring." The order was written "exactly as Haman commanded" and went out under the king's name. I think that's what gave it so much weight.
One day, friend. The order sets it all "…on a single day, the thirteenth day of Adar, the twelfth month." That's the month the lot fell on back in verse 7. It's a hard line to read.

Not those two. The text says the letters "were sent by couriers to each of the royal provinces." As for the king and Haman, the text says, "Then the king and Haman sat down to drink…" Couriers do the traveling.
The queen isn't mentioned in these verses. The text says, "Then the king and Haman sat down to drink…" That's what the king and Haman do once the edict is out.
No party in Susa, friend. The text says the king and Haman sat down to drink, "…but the city of Susa was in confusion." The word is confusion, and that's not celebration.
Silence isn't the word. The text says, "…but the city of Susa was in confusion." Confusion means people were stirred up and unsure.
